The Agency recognizes that some eligibility criteria may have become commonly accepted 36 over time or used as a template across trials, but such criteria should be carefully considered and 37 be appropriate for a specific trial context. Unnecessarily restrictive eligibility criteria may slow 38 subject accrual, limit patients’ access to clinical trials, and lead to trial results that do not fully 39 represent treatment effects in the patient population that will ultimately use the drug. 5 , 6

candidates.statement: Washout periods and concomitant medication exclusions are commonly included in cancer 55 clinical trials. However, these exclusions often vary across trials for similar therapeutic classes 56 and diseases and should be appropriate for the trial under consideration. 57
candidates.context: A washout period is a treatment-free period between the most recent anti-cancer treatment and 59 treatment with the investigational drug. This treatment-free period is intended to allow a prior 60 therapy and/or its effects on the body to be eliminated or reduced to acceptable levels preventing 61 additional toxicity and/or interfering with the pharmacokinetics/pharmacodynamics (PK/PD) of 62 the investigational drug when a new therapy is started. For clinical trials, this is also important to 63 prevent misinterpreting safety or efficacy observations about study-related treatments that could 64 be attributed to prior therapies. candidates.statement: Concomitant medications are any prescription or non-prescription medications (i.e., over-the- 70 counter drugs) a subject may be taking in addition to the investigational drug product(s). 71 Although this guidance is focused on concomitant medications, certain products such as dietary 72 supplements that are not regulated as drugs or biological products may also interfere with drug 73 clearance. Patients receiving anticancer therapies often have comorbidities that require drug 74 therapy or cancer-related issues that require supportive care (e.g., prophylactic antimicrobials or 75 treatment of symptoms related to cancer therapy). Undue restrictions to concomitant medications 76 may result in hindered trial enrollment, as the average patient with cancer takes five chronic non- 77 cancer medications, not including those that may be used to manage adverse events associated 78 with anticancer therapy. 8 The prevalence of comorbidities and associated polypharmacy are 79 more common in older patients, and exclusion of specific concomitant medications could result 80 in preferentially excluding older patients from cancer clinical trials. 9 Exclusion of specific 81 concomitant medications should be scientifically and clinically justified in the context of the 82 known drug profile. Sponsors should consider removing exclusions carried over from earlier 83 trials as increased drug metabolism, clearance, and drug-drug interaction information becomes 84 available and suggests certain concomitant medications should no longer be prohibited. Sponsors 85 may, if applicable, provide alternatives to prohibited concomitant medications in trial protocols. 86

candidates.statement: Eligibility criteria should be tailored to the population being studied and the goals of the clinical 91 investigation. 10 For that reason, the recommendations in this guidance reflect a general approach 92 to broadening eligibility criteria related to washout periods and concomitant medications, rather 93 than providing specific or prescriptive criteria. Exclusion criteria should be justified with a 94 disease- and drug-specific scientific rationale as opposed to vague statements. For example, 95 sponsors should avoid statements such as, “Exclude patients taking concomitant medications 96 expected to increase the risk for a clinically significant adverse event.” 97

candidates.statement: • Relevant clinical and laboratory parameters, based on the characteristics of preceding 110 therapy, should be used in place of time-based washout periods to address safety 111 considerations (e.g., “[laboratory test value] must have returned to within normal 112 limits or acceptable baseline prior to enrollment/initiation of study treatment”). 113
candidates.context: • Time-based washout periods (e.g., “at least 14 days must have elapsed since last 115 treatment with [therapy] before the patient may be enrolled”) should be scientifically 116 justified and relevant PK/PD of the prior therapy should be taken into consideration. 117 If time-based washout periods are included in trial eligibility criteria, justification 118 should be clearly specified in the protocol (e.g., provide data or justification 119 indicating that a washout is needed so that a subject is not exposed to specific 120 unreasonable risks). A washout period may be appropriate if prior therapy can result 121 in delayed anti-tumor effects, if one of the objectives of a trial is an estimate of anti- 122 tumor effects of an investigational drug. 123

candidates.statement: • Patients using concomitant medications should only be excluded from trial 132 participation when clinically relevant known or predicted drug-drug interactions and 133 potential overlapping toxicities will impact the safety of trial subjects. 134

Concomitant Medications 130 • Alternatively, instead of excluding patients using interacting concomitant 136 medications, sponsors may also consider modification of the dosage or regimen of the 137 investigational anti-cancer agent or the concomitant medications. These approaches 138 should be justified and clearly specified in the protocol and other study materials. 139 Subjects and caregivers should be adequately informed of these changes. 140
